title: Monopolistic competition and optimal advertising
summary: The environment of monopolistic competition, limited market power, short-run profit and long-run zero profit, the good, bad and ugly, and the optimal advertising rule.

chunks.heading: Environment and limited market power
chunks.explanation_md:
Think of shampoo brands. There are **numerous sellers\**, and each brand is a little **different\**, so each firm faces a **downward sloping demand curve\**: it can raise its price a bit without losing every customer.

But the brands are **close substitutes\**, so buyers do switch. That makes each firm's demand **more elastic\** than a monopolist's. Add **free entry and exit\**, and the firm has only **limited market power\**.

Like a monopolist, it can price **above MC\**, and its MR lies below its demand curve.
chunks.exam_line: Many firms, differentiated products, free entry: downward sloping demand but limited market power.

check_questions.stem: In monopolistic competition, each firm faces a downward sloping demand curve because:
Other brands make a monopolistically competitive firm's demand more elastic than a monopolist's.

chunks.big_idea: Monopolistic competition is many firms selling slightly different brands: each has a little pricing power, but not much.

chunks.exam_answer_md: Monopolistic competition: numerous buyers and sellers, **differentiated products\** (so each firm faces a downward sloping demand curve, but consumers see brands as close substitutes) and **free entry and exit\** (so zero profits in the long run). Firms can price above MC, but other brands make demand more elastic, so they have **limited market power\**.

chunks.heading: Short run and long run
chunks.explanation_md:
**Short run:** produce where **MR = MC\** and charge the price on the demand curve, exactly like a monopolist. If that price is above ATC, the brand **makes a profit\**.

**Long run:** profit attracts rivals. Their **new brands steal market share\**, so your demand curve **shifts left\** (D to D1). This continues until the demand curve just **touches the AC curve\**: there **P = AC\** and **profit is zero\**.
chunks.exam_line: Short run: MR = MC, possible profit. Long run: entry shifts demand down until P = AC and profit is zero.

check_questions.stem: In long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition:
options: P = AC and profit is zero
P = MC and profit is positive
check_questions.answer: P = AC and profit is zero

check_questions.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm maximizes short-run profit like a monopolist.

chunks.big_idea: In the short run the brand acts like a little monopoly and can profit; in the long run copycats enter until profit is zero.

visuals.title: Long run: demand falls until it just touches AC
visuals.caption: Entry shifts the brand's demand to D1, which touches AC at Q1. There P = AC, so profit is zero, and P is still above MC.

watch_out: In the long run P = AC, but **not** minimum AC. That gap is the excess capacity.
chunks.memory_trick: **Short run like a monopoly, long run like perfect competition (zero profit).**
chunks.exam_answer_md: **Short run:** maximize profits like a monopolist: produce where MR = MC and charge the price on the demand curve; the firm may earn profits. **Long run:** with free entry, rivals enter and new brands steal market share, reducing the firm's demand until profits are zero: **P = AC\**. (Draw the short-run graph with a profit box, and the long-run graph with D1 tangent to AC.)

chunks.heading: The good, the bad and the ugly
chunks.explanation_md:
| For | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Consumers (good)** | Product variety |
| **Society (bad)** | P > MC, excess capacity, unexploited economies of scale |
| **Managers (ugly)** | P = ATC > minimum average cost, and zero profits in the long run |
chunks.exam_line: Good: variety. Bad: P > MC, excess capacity. Ugly: zero long-run profit.

chunks.big_idea: Consumers get variety, society gets waste, and managers get zero long-run profit.

watch_out: Excess capacity is bad for **society**, not for consumers.
chunks.exam_answer_md: **Good (consumers):** product variety. **Bad (society):** P > MC, excess capacity, unexploited economies of scale. **Ugly (managers):** P = ATC > minimum of average costs and zero profits in the long run.

chunks.heading: Optimal advertising
chunks.explanation_md:
Advertising is how firms with market power **differentiate\** their brands. How much to spend?

Keep advertising while the **extra revenue\** from ads is more than the **extra cost\**. Stop where they are equal.

The slide turns this into a ratio: the **advertising-to-sales ratio\** equals the **advertising elasticity\** divided by minus the **own-price elasticity\**:

**A/R = EQ,A / (-EQ,P)**

So if your buyers react strongly to ads (high EQ,A) and weakly to price, spend a bigger share of sales on advertising.

options: Advertising elasticity over minus own-price elasticity
check_questions.answer: Advertising elasticity over minus own-price elasticity

chunks.big_idea: Advertise until one more rupee of ads brings in exactly one more rupee of revenue.
watch_out: The own-price elasticity is negative, so the formula uses **minus** EQ,P to make the ratio positive.
chunks.exam_answer_md: Advertise to the point where the additional revenue from advertising equals its additional cost. Equivalently, the profit-maximizing **advertising-to-sales ratio A/R = EQ,A / (-EQ,P)**.

questions.stem: Product variety under monopolistic competition is good for:
Distinguish between perfect competition and monopolistic competition.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Perfect competition | Monopolistic competition |
|---|---|---|
| Product | Homogeneous | Differentiated |
| Firm's demand | Horizontal, price taker (P = MR) | Downward sloping, limited market power |
| Output rule | P = MC | MR = MC, price from demand, so P > MC |
| Long run | Zero profit, P = minimum AC, efficient plant size | Zero profit, P = AC above minimum average cost, excess capacity |
| Entry and exit | Free | Free |
